judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Content Standards (same grain, same rank 1) in the Number identity scope. B5.1.2.1 covers mental mathematics strategies and number properties for basic multiplication facts to 81 and the related division facts; B5.1.2.4 requires demonstrating understanding of division of a 2- or 3-digit number by a 1- or 2-digit number (its bounded indicator context shows efficient division of 3-digit by 1-digit numbers). Recall and strategic use of basic division/multiplication facts is the computational substrate for multi-digit division procedures, so proficiency in the first substantively supports likely success in the second; the change is from single-fact fluency to multi-digit quotient computation, which is more than word overlap. Direction is same-rank but justified by this substantive escalation in operand size and procedural demand, not by code order alone. Note both endpoints have unresolved ancestry, so no Strand/Sub-Strand hierarchy was used as positive evidence; judgment rests on statement text and source-anchor identity scope only.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same rank 0) in Strand 4: Data, Sub-strand 1 (Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis) under the same Content Standard B4.4.1.1 on many-to-one correspondence in displaying and interpreting graphs, so the grain matches. Beyond shared placement, the statement texts show a pair-specific developmental step: the first (B4.4.1.1.2, LC 'use an understanding of many-to-one correspondence to display or construct graphs') develops the productive skill of constructing/displaying graphs with a many-to-one scale, while the second (B4.4.1.1.3, LCs 'compare graphs in which the same data has been displayed' and 'explain how graphs displaying the same data are the same and different') requires analysing and justifying differences among multiple completed displays of the same data set. Fluency in constructing such graphs and understanding their scale conventions plausibly supports success in comparing and explaining alternative displays, so the forward direction is first_to_second; the reverse is not supported since comparison presupposes familiarity with how the displays are built. Evidence is limited to bounded excerpts with per-SFI source-evidence truncation (24 omitted items each), but the retained statement text and Learning Components are sufficient and non-contradictory.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 Content Standards (same grain, same canonical coordinate rank 2) under Strand 1: Number, but in different sub-strands: B6.1.2.2 (Number Operations) requires demonstrating understanding of multiplication of 2- or 3-digit numbers by 2- or 3-digit numbers, while B6.1.3.1 (Fractions) requires strategies for comparing, adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing common, decimal and percent fractions. Fluent multi-digit whole-number multiplication is the operational basis for the multiplication (and related decimal/percent computation) strategies demanded by the fractions standard, which extends the same operations into a broader and more complex number domain; proficiency in the whole-number standard therefore supports success in the fractions standard. Same-rank direction is justified by this substantive content extension rather than by shared parentage, code prefix, or the generic 'demonstrate understanding of' wording overlap, which alone would not suffice. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated, so the indicator-level detail is only partly visible; the judgment rests on the trustworthy standard statements and Sub-Strand context.

judgment.rationale: Both Indicators sit under Content Standard B4.2.2.2 (Solve one-step equations involving a symbol for an unknown) in Strand 2: Algebra, Sub-strand 2: Unknowns, Expressions and Equations, at the same BASIC 4 coordinate (rank 0), so direction rests on statement content, not rank. B4.2.2.2.3 (first) asks learners to solve an already-given equation with the unknown on either side — a bounded procedural skill (LC: 'Solve a given equation when the unknown is on the left or right side of the equation'). B4.2.2.2.5 (second) requires the added modelling steps of identifying the unknown in a problem, representing that problem with an equation, and then solving it concretely, pictorially or symbolically (LCs: 'Identify the unknown in a problem', 'Represent the problem with an equation', 'Solve the problem concretely, pictorially or symbolically'). The second combines and extends the first: fluency in solving a supplied equation with the unknown in either position supports success when learners must first construct the equation from a problem and then solve it across representations. This is a same-grade substantive extension rather than mere repetition, so buildsTowards first_to_second is supported; endpoint source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), which tempers confidence slightly.

Because the two share the same grade rank and the evidence does not decisively show one is the enabling proficiency for the other (one adds design demand, the other adds repeated trials, recording and explanation; source code ordering and page proximity are not positive developmental evidence), a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment. Both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence (24 omitted items each), so deeper directional evidence may exist outside this bounded excerpt.
